reporting-org.narrative: Defence for Children International Netherlands - ECPAT Netherlands

description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems.

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: - Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years) - Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms. - CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions. - Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC - Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC - International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying - Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public - Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

title.narrative: # of advocacy networks with increased L&A capacities

comment.narrative: In Asia,Alliance Network Members at national and regional level have varied levels of experience, knowledge and capacity to advocate specifically on the role of technology in the sexual exploitation of children, or towards the ICT Sector. Based on priorities defined through consultation with the Alliance, the component in Y1 shaped its focus towards mainstreaming child participation and voices of children and developing an inclusive process engaging all the project partners in advocating for online safety for children. ECPAT brought its existing knowledge and network in Asia and globally to leverage the opportunity of key events in Asia and explore advocacy gaps for the Alliance to address where relevant. The country L&A groups were formed in Y1, therefore the advocacy network is to be strenghten in Y2.On international level, ased on priorities defined through consultation with the country teams of the Alliance in Asia and the Americas, the component in Y1 shaped its focus towards improving cooperation with law enforcement, engaging the private sector and improving laws and policies in relation to effective ways of working with the informal sector, meaningful engagement of children and young people, protecting children’s rights through an international treaty on business and human rights, and the use of extraterritorial laws, including sex offender registries, to protect children from sexual exploitation. ECPAT brought its existing knowledge and network globally to leverage the opportunity of key events and explore advocacy gaps for the Alliance to address where relevant. The country L&A groups were formed in Y1, therefore the advocacy network is to be strenghten in Y2.

Alliance Network Members at national and regional level will have developed knowledge, skills and experience to advocate at regional level specifically on the role of technology in the sexual exploitation of children, or towards the ICT Sector. This will be through a bottom-up and regional-to-national approach whereby more experienced advocates on this topic can lead and guide others. The desired capacity is to work on agreed joint key messaging and approaches reflecting the synergies between the current regional L&A plan and country plans, and to build a stronger collective identity of the Alliance in Y2. The desired capacity is to continue work ing closely together on agreed joint key messaging and approaches reflecting the synergies between the current international L&A plan and country plans, and to build a stronger collective identity of the Alliance in Y2.

In Asia, the L&A strategies and activities were designed through concept notes linked to the programme’s Theory of Change (ToC). The L&A at the regional level has been led by ECPAT International, while countries have been leading local and national level strategies. The L&A efforts are intended to take a comprehensive approach to reach policy domains at different levels to influence laws, policies, regulations, and practices related to ending the sexual exploitation of children. The L&A capacity is measured by the level of alignment of communication pathways and engagement of country leads. The desired future capacity has not been reached yet, it needs to build on the agreed key communication messages resulting from Y1. At International level, the L&A strategies and activities were designed through concept notes linked to the programme’s Theory of Change (ToC). The L&A has been led by ECPAT International, while countries have been leading local and national level strategies. The L&A efforts are intended to take a comprehensive approach to reach policy domains at different levels to influence laws, policies, regulations, and practices related to ending the sexual exploitation of children. The L&A capacity is measured by the level of alignment of communication pathways and engagement of country leads and global presence of the Alliance. The desired future capacity has not been reached yet, it needs to be strenghten based on the developed evidence and common messages in Y1.
